title: Advanced Join Patterns
objective: After this lesson you will be able to join a table to itself, join on ranges instead of equality, predict and diagnose row fanout, and choose the correct join shape for multi-path questions — all in flat, sandbox-runnable SQL.
why: INNER and LEFT JOIN (Fundamentals) cover the happy path. Real schemas ask harder questions: 'developers in the same country' (a table meeting itself), 'courses priced within a band of each other', 'why did my 14 developers become 28 rows'. This lesson is the difference between knowing join syntax and reasoning about what joins do to row counts — the skill interviewers probe first.

blocks.text: A **self-join** joins a table to itself under two different aliases — conceptually two copies side by side. The trigger phrase is *pairs within one table*: developers sharing a country, courses in the same topic, employees and their managers. Aliases aren't cosmetic here; they are how the engine tells the two copies apart.

blocks.code:
-- Pairs of developers from the same country (each pair once, nobody paired with themselves)
SELECT a.name AS dev_a, b.name AS dev_b, a.country
FROM developers a
JOIN developers b
  ON a.country = b.country
 AND a.id < b.id
ORDER BY a.country;
blocks.caption: Self-join: two aliases, equality on the shared trait, inequality to dedupe pairs

blocks.text: The `a.id < b.id` condition does two jobs: it excludes self-pairs (nobody with themselves) and it collapses mirror duplicates (Maya–Jonas and Jonas–Maya become one row). Without it you get every pair twice plus identity rows — the most common self-join bug, and it looks correct until you count.

Join conditions don't have to be equality — any predicate works, including ranges. The classic is **banding**: match each row to the bracket it falls in (hours → pace bands, prices → tiers). Write the bands as a small inline table of values and join with `BETWEEN`.

blocks.code:
-- Band each developer into a pace tier via a range join
SELECT d.name, d.hours_studied, bands.pace
FROM developers d
JOIN (
  SELECT 'ramping' AS pace, 0 AS lo, 399 AS hi
  UNION ALL SELECT 'steady', 400, 799
  UNION ALL SELECT 'deep', 800, 999999
) AS bands
  ON d.hours_studied BETWEEN bands.lo AND bands.hi
ORDER BY d.hours_studied DESC;
blocks.caption: Non-equi join in real PostgreSQL/SQLite — bands as data, matched by range

blocks.text: This is Chapter 4's bucketing expressed relationally: bands live in rows instead of WHEN clauses, so adding a tier means inserting a row, not editing logic. (The branch table uses UNION ALL stacking from Chapter 3 — the chapters compose deliberately.) Prefer bands-as-data when thresholds change often or are user-configured; prefer CASE when they are fixed analytics definitions.

blocks.title: Sandbox note
blocks.text: The sandbox engine runs flat SELECT with JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY and ORDER BY. Self-joins and the flat pieces of this lesson run there; UNION ALL-stacked branch tables and other multi-statement shapes target real SQLite/PostgreSQL. Verify each half in the sandbox, assemble in a real database.

**Fanout** is row multiplication: when the right side matches a left row N times, that left row appears N times. One developer with 3 enrollments contributes 3 joined rows — so `COUNT(*)` after a join counts *matches*, not developers. Every 'my totals doubled overnight' bug is fanout, and the diagnosis is always the same: aggregate *before* joining, or count distinct keys.

blocks.caption: Fanout diagnosis: COUNT(*) counts matches, COUNT(DISTINCT key) counts entities

blocks.text: The deeper fix is ordering operations: pre-aggregate the many-side in a CTE or derived table (Chapters 1–2), *then* join one-row-per-key. `COUNT(DISTINCT)` rescues a metric; restructuring rescues the query. When totals look inflated, your first suspect is always an unexamined join.

rows: Counts doubled after adding a join
COUNT(DISTINCT key), or aggregate before joining
Add the strict inequality on the key
BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends; overlapping bands
Make bands adjacent non-overlapping; test boundary rows
No match on the right side discards the row
LEFT JOIN + IS NULL check, or confirm absence is intended

blocks.text: Multi-path joins: two roads to the same table

Some questions join the same table twice along different paths — enrollments once for completions, courses once for titles, developers once for names. Each join needs its own alias and its own ON clause; each answers a different relationship. Read multi-join queries as a chain of relationships ('developer → their enrollments → each enrollment's course'), and verify each link's cardinality before trusting the totals.

blocks.code:
-- Full learning story per enrollment: who, what, how far — one row per enrollment
SELECT d.name AS learner, c.title AS course, e.progress,
       CASE WHEN e.completed = 1 THEN 'done' ELSE 'in progress' END AS status
FROM enrollments e
JOIN developers d ON d.id = e.developer_id
JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
ORDER BY e.progress DESC
LIMIT 10;
blocks.caption: Multi-path join for real SQLite/PostgreSQL (CASE labels the status)

blocks.query: SELECT a.name AS dev_a, b.name AS dev_b, a.country FROM developers a JOIN developers b ON a.country = b.country AND a.id < b.id ORDER BY a.country;
blocks.note: Run this self-join in the sandbox — flat joins run here. Count the pairs, then remove the AND a.id < b.id clause and re-run: watch mirrors and self-pairs appear. That contrast is the lesson.

items: Self-join with two aliases for within-table pairs; a.id < b.id kills mirrors and self-pairs
Non-equi joins match on ranges — bands-as-data beats CASE when thresholds change
Fanout multiplies rows per match: COUNT(*) counts matches, COUNT(DISTINCT key) counts entities, pre-aggregation fixes the query
Multi-path joins chain relationships — verify each link's cardinality before trusting totals
Flat join pieces run in the sandbox; stacked/CTE assemblies target real SQLite/PostgreSQL

exercise.prompt: Find 'study buddies': pairs of developers at the SAME level with hours_studied within 100 of each other (excluding self-pairs and mirrors). Return dev_a, dev_b, level, and the hour gap, closest pairs first. Build and verify it in the sandbox, then in one sentence say which join features make this impossible with a single-table WHERE.
hints: Self-join developers AS a and developers AS b. Same level is equality (a.level = b.level); closeness is a range on a computed difference.
Gap = ABS(a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) — sandbox check: does the engine accept ABS? If not, use the two-sided form a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied BETWEEN -100 AND 100.
Dedupe with a.id < b.id, filter gap <= 100, ORDER BY the gap ascending.
exercise.solution:
SELECT a.name AS dev_a, b.name AS dev_b, a.level,
  ABS(a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) AS gap
FROM developers a
JOIN developers b
  ON a.level = b.level
 AND a.id < b.id
WHERE ABS(a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) <= 100
ORDER BY gap;
exercise.why: Three join features combine: equality (same level), computed range (closeness), and key inequality (dedupe). A single-table WHERE can filter rows but cannot pair them — pairing needs two row variables, which only a self-join provides. The one-sentence answer: WHERE sees one row at a time, so cross-row relationships require the table to meet itself.
exercise.code:
-- Sandbox version (verify here): two-sided range avoids ABS
SELECT a.name AS dev_a, b.name AS dev_b, a.level,
  (a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) AS gap
FROM developers a
JOIN developers b
  ON a.level = b.level
 AND a.id < b.id
WHERE (a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) BETWEEN -100 AND 100
ORDER BY gap;

-- Real-DB version with ABS (cleaner, same rows up to sign):
SELECT a.name AS dev_a, b.name AS dev_b, a.level,
  ABS(a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) AS gap
FROM developers a
JOIN developers b
  ON a.level = b.level
 AND a.id < b.id
WHERE ABS(a.hours_studied - b.hours_studied) <= 100
ORDER BY gap;

quiz.q: A self-join of developers on country without any id condition returns mirrors and self-pairs. What does AND a.id < b.id achieve?
options: It speeds up the query via the primary key
It keeps each unordered pair exactly once and excludes identity pairs
It restricts results to adjacent ids
It converts the join to a LEFT JOIN
quiz.explain: For any two distinct rows exactly one ordering satisfies id_a < id_b, so each pair survives once; a row never satisfies id < id against itself. Ordering by an uncorrelated unique key is the standard pair-dedupe.

quiz.q: After adding a join, COUNT(*) doubles but COUNT(DISTINCT d.id) stays correct. Diagnosis?
options: The database double-counts joined queries by design
Fanout: right-side rows match multiple times, so COUNT(*) counts matches, not entities
DISTINCT is required on all joined queries
quiz.explain: Each left row repeats per right-side match. COUNT(*) tallies the repetitions; COUNT(DISTINCT key) tallies entities. The structural cure is aggregating the many-side before joining.

quiz.q: When should bands live in rows (range join) instead of WHEN clauses (CASE)?
options: When thresholds change often or are user-configured: adding a tier becomes a data edit, not a logic edit
When there are more than 100 rows
quiz.explain: Data-driven bands are maintainable by non-SQL edits and auditable as rows. Fixed analytic definitions belong in CASE. Same buckets, different change dynamics — choose by who changes them and how often.

quiz.q: Why can't a single-table WHERE find 'developers within 100 hours of each other'?
options: WHERE evaluates one row at a time — cross-row comparison needs two row variables, i.e. a self-join
It can — the premise is false
quiz.explain: WHERE filters rows independently; 'within X of each other' relates pairs. The self-join introduces the second row variable (a and b) that makes the relationship expressible.

summary: Self-joins pair rows within one table (dedupe with key inequality), non-equi joins match ranges (bands-as-data for changing thresholds), fanout explains every mysteriously doubled total, and multi-path joins chain relationships link by link. Verify joins in the sandbox; assemble stacks in a real database.
next: Joined rows answer questions — but reusable logic needs a home. Next: views, the persistent named queries that turn Chapter 2's pipelines into database objects.
